newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan condemns Jerusalem tunnel opening.
newsitem.headline: Jordan condemns Jerusalem tunnel opening.

text.p: Crown Prince Hassan of Jordan said Israel had violated the sanctity of the holy city of Jerusalem and provoked Moslems around the world by opening a tunnel beside the Temple Mount, site of Islam's third holiest site.
Israel's move was "a provocation to Arab and Moslem feelings around the world", the crown prince said in a statement carried by the state news agency Petra on Tuesday night.
In the strongly worded statement from Israel's closest Arab peace partner, Hassan warned Israeli authorities against disregarding Moslem attachment to the holy city.
"It was a cause of wars just as much as it is a unifying symbol for peace," said Hassan, regent in the absence of his brother King Hussein.

Palestinians clashed with police in Jerusalem on Tuesday after workmen opened the tunnel under cover of night. The PLO said the tunnel is part of a programme to Judaise Jerusalem and the Arab League has warned it will ignite Arab anger.
In London, an Israeli spokesman travelling with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Hassan had called the Israeli leader on Wednesday seeking an explanation.

"The prime minister made it clear to him that the tunnel does not go under the Temple Mount. It won't collapse the Temple Mount. It is an incredible historic project," spokesman Shai Bazak told reporters.
Bazak said Netanyahu told Hassan the tunnel would benefit all residents of the Old City, Arabs and Jews alike, and Hassan responded that Israel should make this known.

Jordan lost the walled old city of Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East War when Israeli forces captured the West Bank. But the 1994 Jordanian-Israeli peace treaty acknowledged a special role for Jordan in maintaining Jerusalem's Moslem sites.

"Jordan will persist in exerting efforts to spotlight this new political crisis in the life of the holy city," Hassan, who has postponed a planned visit to Jerusalem early next month, said in Tuesday's statement.
The trip, only his second since attending the funeral of slain Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin last year, was put off because of "overburdened schedules", a palace spokesman said on Tuesday.

A government statement, also carried by Petra, condemned the opening of the tunnel "which undermines the structure of Al-Aqsa mosque, changes the features of the holy city, and harms the feelings of Arabs and Moslems."
It called on the Israeli government to stick to international agreements and urged Arab and Islamic states to work to "preserve the holy city and not to harm the Al-Aqsa mosque."
